course.title: Education
course.desc: Lesson plans, student feedback, rubric creation, parent communication.

exercises.title: Vague vs. precise
exercises.sc:
You need a lesson plan for tomorrow's 8th-grade science class on photosynthesis. Here's what most teachers type:

"Create a lesson plan on photosynthesis."

The AI returns a generic overview that doesn't match your 50-minute block, your students' reading levels, or the NGSS standards you need to cover.
exercises.task: Write a better prompt. Be specific about: grade level, time constraints, learning objectives aligned to NGSS MS-LS1-6, student prior knowledge, and what activities to include. Imagine you have 28 students with mixed reading levels.
exercises.hint: The guide's principle: a 200-word specification produces better results than a 20-word instruction followed by 15 rounds of correction.
exercises.cr: 1) Specifies grade level and class duration 2) References specific standards (e.g., NGSS MS-LS1-6) 3) Defines learning objectives 4) Mentions student context or prior knowledge 5) Is substantially more detailed than 'create a lesson plan on photosynthesis'

exercises.title: Specify the output
exercises.sc: Your department chair asks you to "get the AI to analyze our students' Q1 grade data." You have grades for 4 sections of 10th-grade English across 5 assignment types: essays, quizzes, participation, projects, and exams.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that specifies exactly what the output should look like. Define the structure — table? Bullet points? What columns, metrics, comparisons? Think about what your department chair actually needs to see.
exercises.hint: If you handed the output to your department chair, would they immediately know what they're looking at without follow-up questions?
exercises.cr: 1) Specifies output format explicitly 2) Names specific metrics (averages, pass rates, distributions) 3) Requests comparisons across sections or assignment types 4) Defines what 'good' looks like for the analysis

exercises.title: Audience and tone
exercises.sc:
A 7th-grade student, Marcus, has been struggling with reading comprehension and his grade dropped from B to D-. You need to communicate this to:

1. Marcus's parents (supportive, solution-oriented)
2. The school principal (data-driven, professional)
3. Marcus himself (encouraging, age-appropriate)
exercises.task: Write a prompt for ONE audience that explicitly controls tone, length, and emphasis. Make it clear who the reader is and what they care about.
exercises.hint: Parents want to know 'what's happening and how can we help.' Administrators want data and intervention plans. Students need encouragement plus clear next steps.
exercises.cr: 1) Clearly identifies target audience 2) Specifies tone 3) Defines what to emphasize vs. omit 4) Sets length expectations 5) Shows audience-aware framing

exercises.title: Setting constraints
exercises.sc: You're asking the AI to create a curriculum document for your 5th-grade math unit on fractions aligned to CCSS 5.NF. Without constraints, the AI produces either a half-page outline or a 20-page textbook chapter with content beyond grade level.
exercises.task: Write a prompt with explicit constraints: page count, what NOT to include, required sections, formatting rules, and standards alignment requirements.
exercises.hint: Telling the AI what to avoid is just as valuable as telling it what to do. For example: 'Do not include fraction multiplication — that's Unit 4.'
exercises.cr: 1) Sets specific length constraint 2) Includes 'do not' instructions (e.g., excluding certain topics) 3) Lists required sections 4) Mentions specific standards alignment (CCSS 5.NF) 5) Demonstrates negative constraints

exercises.title: Role assignment
exercises.sc: You wrote a peer observation feedback report for a colleague's 9th-grade algebra class. You could ask the AI to "review this feedback" — but the quality depends on what perspective the AI takes.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that assigns the AI a specific role (e.g., "You are an instructional coach with 12 years of experience in secondary math education and a focus on formative assessment strategies"). Define what expertise to apply.
exercises.hint: A 'curriculum specialist' catches different things than a 'student engagement expert' or a 'new teacher mentor.'
exercises.cr: 1) Assigns a specific role with credentials 2) Defines what expertise to apply 3) Specifies what to evaluate in the feedback 4) Role choice meaningfully shapes the review

exercises.title: Iterative refinement
exercises.sc:
You asked the AI for a student progress report and got:

"Marcus is doing okay in class. He participates sometimes and turns in most assignments. He could improve in some areas."

Generic, vague, useless for a parent conference.
exercises.task: Write a follow-up prompt that fixes this. Don't start over — refine. Tell the AI specifically what's wrong and what to change.
exercises.hint: Good refinement is surgical: 'Replace "participates sometimes" with specific data — Marcus contributed to 3 of 12 group discussions this quarter.' Bad: 'Make it more detailed.'
exercises.cr: 1) References specific problems in the original 2) Gives targeted corrections 3) Adds missing specifics (grades, examples, data) 4) Shows refinement over restarting 5) Demonstrates iterate cycle

exercises.title: Plan before you ask
exercises.sc:
You need a comprehensive unit plan for a 3-week 11th-grade AP US History unit on the Civil Rights Movement. If you just say "write a unit plan on the Civil Rights Movement," you'll get mediocre results.

The guide's core principle: spend 10 minutes planning to save an hour of corrections.
exercises.task: Write a detailed specification prompt (150-250 words). Include: learning objectives tied to AP framework, target student profile, required primary sources, assessment types, daily breakdown, differentiation strategies, and exclusions.
exercises.hint: Your specification IS the prompt. The more precise the spec, the better the first output.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines learning objectives tied to standards/framework 2) Lists specific topics and primary sources 3) Specifies assessment types 4) Sets daily/weekly breakdown 5) Includes differentiation 6) Spec itself is 100+ words

exercises.title: Chain-of-thought
exercises.sc: A student, Priya, is performing inconsistently: A on essays, D on quizzes, B+ on projects, F on the midterm exam. Her parents want to understand what's going on. You need the AI to analyze her learning profile rather than just averaging grades.
exercises.task: Write a prompt forcing step-by-step thinking: first categorize each assessment type by the skill it measures, then identify patterns in Priya's strengths and weaknesses, then hypothesize root causes, then recommend interventions. Use explicit step numbering.
exercises.hint: Chain-of-thought: 'Before giving your answer, first do X, then Y, then Z.' Reasoning improves dramatically with sequential steps.
exercises.cr: 1) Uses explicit numbered steps 2) Separates data extraction from analysis 3) Asks for reasoning before conclusions 4) Includes hypothesis generation 5) Steps build logically from data to recommendation

exercises.title: Few-shot examples
exercises.sc:
You're grading 30 student essays on "The Impact of the Industrial Revolution" using a 4-point rubric. You need the AI to grade consistently, matching your standards.

Examples from your grading:
• "The Industrial Revolution changed everything" (no evidence, vague claim) → 1/4
• "Factory conditions were harsh, as shown by 16-hour workdays for children as young as 5" (specific evidence, clear argument) → 3/4
• "The textile industry's shift from hand looms to power looms between 1760-1840 displaced 250,000 workers, creating the first urban poverty crisis" (precise data, causal analysis, historical context) → 4/4
exercises.task: Write a prompt using few-shot examples that teaches the AI to grade new essays consistently. Include examples for each rubric level, define the scoring criteria, and add 2-3 student essay excerpts as test cases.
exercises.hint: Format consistency matters: if examples use '→', use '→' for all of them. Each score level needs a clear example showing WHY it earned that score.
exercises.cr: 1) Includes 3+ clear example pairs 2) Defines all rubric levels 3) Examples cover multiple score levels 4) Includes new test cases 5) Consistent format throughout

exercises.title: Structured output
exercises.sc:
You've been asked to create an assessment rubric for a 10th-grade biology lab report. Instead of a paragraph description, you want a structured assessment matrix:

| Criterion | Exemplary (4) | Proficient (3) | Developing (2) | Beginning (1) |
exercises.task: Write a prompt that enforces specific output structure. Define exact columns, what goes in each cell, how many criteria to include, and how to handle edge cases like incomplete lab reports.
exercises.hint: Show the exact format you want. Include an example row if possible — for instance, the 'Hypothesis' criterion fully filled out.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines exact table structure 2) Explains what goes in each cell 3) Specifies number of criteria 4) Handles edge cases 5) Optionally includes example row

exercises.title: Compare and evaluate
exercises.sc:
Two teachers propose different approaches for a struggling 4th-grade reading group:

Approach A: "Pull-out guided reading groups 3x/week, 20 minutes, leveled readers, teacher-led."

Approach B: "In-class peer reading buddies daily, 15 minutes, student-choice books, with reading response journals."
exercises.task: Write a prompt that evaluates both approaches against specific criteria and recommends one. Define 3-4 criteria, ask for per-criterion scores, require justified recommendation with research basis.
exercises.hint: Don't ask 'which is better?' Instead: 'Score each 1-5 on differentiation, student engagement, feasibility with limited staff, and evidence base.'
exercises.cr: 1) Defines 3+ evaluation criteria 2) Asks for per-criterion scores 3) Requires reasoning for each score 4) Requests justified recommendation 5) Criteria are meaningful and non-overlapping

exercises.title: Multi-step decomposition
exercises.sc:
Your principal asks: "Design a new STEM curriculum for grades 6-8, aligned to NGSS, with project-based learning, cross-curricular connections to ELA, and differentiation for our 22% ELL population."

Too big for one prompt. Needs decomposition.
exercises.task: Write a SEQUENCE of 3-4 prompts that decompose this. Each builds on the previous output. Show the full chain.
exercises.hint: Workflow: Standards mapping → Scope and sequence → Unit design with PBL → Differentiation and ELL scaffolds. Each step has clear input and output.
exercises.cr: 1) Breaks into 3+ sequential prompts 2) Each has focused objective 3) Later prompts reference earlier outputs 4) Covers standards→design→differentiation 5) Demonstrates decomposition

exercises.title: Error correction
exercises.sc:
The AI graded a batch of 8th-grade persuasive essays and produced this summary:

"Class average: B+. Most students demonstrated strong persuasive writing. Main weakness: some essays lacked conclusions. Recommendation: reteach essay structure."

Problems: no individual variation noted, ignores rubric dimensions, oversimplifies the weakness, generic recommendation.
exercises.task: Write a prompt correcting these errors. Ask for per-student breakdown, multi-dimensional rubric analysis, pattern identification across specific rubric criteria, and targeted intervention recommendations.
exercises.hint: Point out exactly what's wrong: 'You collapsed 30 unique performances into one average. Break out scores by rubric dimension: thesis, evidence, counterargument, organization, conventions.'
exercises.cr: 1) Identifies specific errors in the original 2) Asks for per-student or disaggregated data 3) Requires multi-dimensional analysis 4) Requests targeted recommendations 5) Shows critical evaluation of AI output

exercises.title: Persona prompting
exercises.sc:
An IEP (Individualized Education Program) meeting is coming up for a 6th-grader with ADHD and reading difficulties. You want to prepare by considering multiple perspectives:

1. Special education teacher (accommodation strategies)
2. School counselor (social-emotional needs)
3. Parent advocate (home-school connection)
4. Reading specialist (intervention approaches)
exercises.task: Write a prompt that has the AI adopt each persona sequentially, evaluate the student's current IEP goals, identify gaps, then synthesize into unified recommendations for the IEP meeting.
exercises.hint: Each persona surfaces different concerns. The SpEd teacher focuses on accommodations, the counselor on behavior and emotions, the parent on what works at home, the specialist on reading interventions.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines 3+ distinct personas with specific expertise 2) Each has specific concerns to address 3) Sequential analysis from each perspective 4) Requests synthesis across all perspectives 5) Shows how persona shapes the analysis

exercises.title: Prompt templates
exercises.sc: Every quarter you write report card comments for 120+ students. Each comment needs to be personalized, reference specific achievements, note areas for growth, and match your school's tone guidelines. Instead of writing a new prompt for each student, you want a reusable template.
exercises.task: Create a reusable prompt template with [BRACKET] variables. Include: student name, subject, grade level, specific achievements, areas for growth, tone, and length. Should work for any student in any subject.
exercises.hint: Variables like [STUDENT_NAME], [SUBJECT], [ACHIEVEMENT_1], [GROWTH_AREA] make it reusable. One template for 120 students saves hours every quarter.
exercises.cr: 1) Uses clear bracket variables 2) Genuinely reusable across students and subjects 3) Covers input/processing/output 4) 4+ variable placeholders 5) Would save significant time each quarter

exercises.title: Curriculum mapping
exercises.sc: Your district adopted new ELA standards and you need to map your existing 9th-grade English curriculum to the updated CCSS ELA standards. You have 6 units, 45 lesson plans, and need to identify gaps, redundancies, and alignment issues before the school board presentation next month.
exercises.task: Write a prompt producing a structured curriculum analysis: standards coverage matrix, gap identification, redundancy flags, and realignment recommendations with priority levels.
exercises.hint: Structure your prompt like a professional curriculum audit: what to extract from existing plans, how to map to standards, how to present findings.
exercises.cr: 1) Lists specific standards to map against 2) Defines gap and redundancy criteria 3) Specifies matrix output format 4) Includes priority-level recommendations 5) Covers all units systematically 6) Professional output suitable for board presentation

exercises.title: Assignment triage
exercises.sc: It's midterm week and you have 147 ungraded assignments across 4 classes: 35 research papers (due back Friday), 42 lab reports (overdue by 3 days), 38 reading responses (students need feedback for next assignment), and 32 quizzes (auto-scored but need review for partial credit).
exercises.task: Write a prompt that categorizes and prioritizes your grading queue. Define priority criteria, estimated time per type, and a scannable schedule that fits your available hours this week.
exercises.hint: Priority Matrix: What impacts students most? What's overdue? What blocks their next assignment? What can be batch-processed fastest?
exercises.cr: 1) Defines triage categories 2) Specifies priority criteria (impact, overdue, blocking) 3) Distinguishes urgent/important grading 4) Creates scannable schedule 5) Practical time-saver for real teacher workload

exercises.title: Faculty meeting notes
exercises.sc: 75-minute faculty meeting. Topics: new state testing schedule, PBIS behavior data review, professional development day planning, budget cuts to electives program, and a new student cell phone policy proposal. Decisions made, action items assigned to various department heads.
exercises.task: Write a prompt transforming rough meeting notes into structured minutes: sections by topic, decisions vs. discussion items, action items with owners and deadlines, and follow-up needed.
exercises.hint: Template: Header with date/attendees, Decisions Made, Action Items (owner + deadline), Discussion Summary by topic, Next Meeting Agenda items.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines output sections 2) Action items have owner + deadline 3) Separates decisions from discussion 4) Handles multiple topics cleanly 5) Includes follow-up items or next meeting agenda

exercises.title: Program cost comparison
exercises.sc:
Your school is evaluating three options for a new reading intervention program:
• Lexia PowerUp: $12,500/year site license, requires 30 Chromebooks ($250 each), 2hr teacher training
• Wilson Reading System: $3,200 for materials + $4,800 per teacher trained (need 3 teachers), ongoing certification
• Hire a part-time reading specialist: $35/hr, 20 hrs/week, 36 weeks/year

Need a 3-year total cost comparison with projected student outcomes.
exercises.task: Write a prompt for a structured cost-benefit comparison: time horizon, all cost categories, explicit assumptions about student outcomes, and recommendation format for the school board.
exercises.hint: Include: initial costs, recurring costs, training time, opportunity costs, projected students served, cost-per-student, and outcome evidence. State all assumptions.
exercises.cr: 1) All cost categories identified 2) Clear 3-year timeframe 3) Explicit assumptions about outcomes and usage 4) Summary comparison table 5) Recommendation with reasoning 6) Cost-per-student dimension

exercises.title: Accreditation report
exercises.sc: Your school's accreditation visit is in 4 months. The accreditation team needs a self-study report covering: mission alignment, student achievement data, curriculum quality, teacher qualifications, school culture, and improvement plans. The report must be evidence-based and 15-20 pages.
exercises.task: Write the specification prompt — the detailed brief for a professional accreditation self-study report section on the first try. Structure, length per section, data requirements, tone, and exclusions.
exercises.hint: This is the ultimate 'plan before you ask' exercise. 200-word spec > 20-word instruction + 15 corrections.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines report structure matching accreditation standards 2) Length per section 3) Data/evidence requirements 4) Professional, evidence-based tone 5) Exclusions 6) Spec is 150+ words 7) Would produce accreditation-ready output

exercises.title: Sensitive communications
exercises.sc:
A 10th-grade student, Devon, has been placed on academic probation after failing 3 of 5 classes. There's also a pending disciplinary referral for repeated class disruptions. You need:
1. Letter to parents (serious but collaborative)
2. Academic improvement plan for Devon (clear, structured)
3. Documentation for the student's file (factual, legally careful)
exercises.task: Write one prompt producing all three documents with different tones but consistent facts. Address the sensitive nature — this is a student's future.
exercises.hint: Facts identical across documents, framing changes. Parent letter: partnership. Improvement plan: student-facing with achievable goals. File documentation: neutral, factual, no subjective language.
exercises.cr: 1) Requests all three documents 2) Different tones for each 3) Consistent facts across all 4) Addresses sensitivity appropriately 5) Handles legal/documentation concerns 6) Strategic communication

exercises.title: Teacher candidate evaluation
exercises.sc: Hiring a new 7th-grade math teacher. Requirements: state certification, 2+ years teaching experience, strong classroom management, experience with differentiated instruction, and comfort with educational technology. 10 applications to screen, shortlist top 3 for demo lessons.
exercises.task: Write a prompt creating systematic screening: scored criteria with weights, must-have vs nice-to-have qualifications, red flags, and shortlist output format.
exercises.hint: Chain-of-thought: extract qualifications → verify certification → score against criteria → rank → recommend. Weighted scoring prevents gut-feel bias in hiring.
exercises.cr: 1) Scored criteria with weights 2) Must-haves vs nice-to-haves 3) Red flags specific to teaching 4) Comparison table 5) Reasoning behind rankings 6) Multiple techniques combined

exercises.title: Student performance analysis
exercises.sc:
End of semester: you have grade data for 150 students across 5 sections of 9th-grade English, plus reading level assessments, attendance records, and behavior referral data. The principal wants:
1. Identify at-risk students
2. Find patterns in performance gaps
3. Recommend targeted interventions
4. Present findings to the department
exercises.task: Write a comprehensive prompt for this end-to-end analysis pipeline. Use few-shot for risk classification, chain-of-thought for pattern analysis, structured output for the report, and persona prompting for the department presentation.
exercises.hint: Capstone: combine every technique. Few-shot + structured output + chain-of-thought + planning + persona.
exercises.cr: 1) Few-shot examples for risk classification 2) Clear risk categories 3) Pattern identification with chain-of-thought 4) Prioritized interventions 5) Structured report output 6) 3+ techniques combined 7) Reusable semester-over-semester

CURRICULUM UNIT CONTEXT

5th-Grade Math: Fractions Unit (Unit 3 of 6)
Duration: 4 weeks (20 instructional days)
Standards: CCSS 5.NF.A.1, 5.NF.A.2

CCSS 5.NF.A.1: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions.

CCSS 5.NF.A.2: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators.

- 4 students identified as gifted
- 3 ELL students (Spanish-speaking, intermediate fluency)

materials.9:
STUDENT ESSAY EXCERPTS TO GRADE

Rubric: 4-point scale
Topic: "The Impact of the Industrial Revolution on Society"

PREVIOUSLY GRADED EXAMPLES:

Score 1/4: "The Industrial Revolution changed everything. People moved to cities and things were different. It was a big deal for everyone."
Why 1: No specific evidence, entirely vague claims, no analysis

Score 2/4: "The Industrial Revolution led to urbanization. Many people left farms to work in factories. Working conditions were often poor and hours were long."
Why 2: General claims with some direction but no specific evidence, dates, or data

Score 3/4: "Factory conditions were harsh, as shown by 16-hour workdays for children as young as 5. The Factory Act of 1833 attempted to address child labor but enforcement was limited."
Why 3: Specific evidence and historical reference, clear argument, but limited analysis of broader impact

Score 4/4: "The textile industry's shift from hand looms to power looms between 1760-1840 displaced 250,000 workers, creating the first urban poverty crisis. This displacement fueled both the Luddite movement and eventually the labor reforms of the 1840s, demonstrating how technological disruption drives social and political change."
Why 4: Precise data, causal analysis, historical context, connects specific evidence to broader themes

NEW ESSAYS TO GRADE:

Student A: "The Industrial Revolution was when factories started. It began in England and spread to other countries. Many inventions were created during this time period that we still use today."

Student B: "Between 1790 and 1830, cotton production in British mills increased from 5 million to 250 million pounds annually. This explosive growth demanded a massive labor force, pulling families from rural communities into cramped urban centers like Manchester, whose population tripled from 25,000 to 75,000 in just 30 years."

Student C: "The Industrial Revolution had both positive and negative effects. On one hand, it created new jobs and products. On the other hand, pollution increased and workers were treated badly. Overall, it was a complicated time in history."
materials.10:
LAB REPORT ASSESSMENT CONTEXT

Course: 10th-Grade Biology
Lab: Enzyme Activity (Effect of Temperature on Catalase)
Standard: NGSS HS-LS1-6 (Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for how carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen from sugar molecules may combine with other elements to form amino acids and/or other large carbon-based molecules)

Lab report sections to assess:
1. Hypothesis
2. Procedure (followed from handout, assess completeness)
3. Data Collection (table with temperatures: 4°C, 22°C, 37°C, 50°C, 70°C)
4. Data Analysis (graph + written interpretation)
5. Conclusion (claim-evidence-reasoning format)
6. Error Analysis

Edge cases to address:
- Student who was absent for lab day but completed write-up from partner's data
- Student who collected data but didn't finish conclusion
- Student who has excellent analysis but data table has errors
- Student who copied procedure verbatim from handout without adaptation
materials.11:
READING INTERVENTION APPROACHES

APPROACH A: Pull-out Guided Reading Groups
- Frequency: 3x per week, 20 minutes per session
- Method: Teacher-led, leveled readers (Fountas & Pinnell)
- Group size: 4-5 students per group
- Staffing: Requires reading specialist or trained teacher
- Evidence base: What Works Clearinghouse rates guided reading as having "moderate" evidence
- Pros: Targeted instruction, immediate feedback
- Cons: Students miss classroom instruction, stigma of being pulled out

APPROACH B: In-Class Peer Reading Buddies
- Frequency: Daily, 15 minutes
- Method: Student-choice books, paired reading with response journals
- Pairing: Higher reader with lower reader (mixed ability)
- Staffing: Classroom teacher monitors, no additional staff needed
- Evidence base: Peer-assisted learning strategies show "strong" evidence (WWC)
- Pros: No pull-out stigma, daily practice, student autonomy
- Cons: Dependent on buddy quality, less targeted instruction

OPTION A - Lexia PowerUp (Software-Based):
- Year 1: $12,500 site license + 30 Chromebooks ($250 each) = $20,000

- Teacher training: 2 hours (included in license)
- Students served: Up to 200
- Implementation: Students use 20 min/day independently
- Evidence: WWC rated, moderate evidence of effectiveness
- Data: Built-in progress monitoring and reports
- Staffing: Minimal — teacher monitors, software adapts

OPTION B - Wilson Reading System (Instructor-Led):
- Year 1: $3,200 materials + $4,800/teacher training x 3 teachers = $17,600
- Year 2-3: $1,200/year consumable materials + $2,400 recertification
- Teacher training: 4 full days initial + ongoing coaching
- Students served: 15-20 per trained teacher (45-60 total)
- Implementation: 45-min sessions, 4-5x/week, small groups of 3-5
- Evidence: WWC rated, strong evidence for students with reading disabilities
- Data: Manual progress monitoring with Wilson assessments
- Staffing: Requires 3 dedicated trained teachers

OPTION C - Part-Time Reading Specialist:
- Year 1-3: $35/hr x 20 hrs/week x 36 weeks = $25,200/year
- Benefits: None (part-time contractor)
- Students served: 20-30 (individual and small group)
- Implementation: Flexible — can use multiple intervention approaches
- Evidence: Dependent on specialist's training and methods
- Data: Specialist creates own monitoring system
- Staffing: 1 specialist, but may have availability/consistency issues
